subsection: 7. Culture, religion and science: identities, the Synod of Thurles, the creative arts and science

notes.h: Catholic identity and the devotional revolution
notes.b: From the 1840s the Catholic Church in Ireland was reorganised and its practice became more uniform, a process historians call the devotional revolution.
points: Church building expanded sharply after 1830, and many large churches and cathedrals were built, often with money raised from the parishes and the Catholic Rent.
Religious orders and congregations grew in number, and women's orders in particular ran schools, hospitals and orphanages.
Devotional practices such as Sunday Mass attendance, confession, the rosary and the cult of the Sacred Heart became more widespread, and parish life became more regular.
The Catholic clergy, now largely drawn from seminaries in Maynooth and in Rome, were better educated and more closely disciplined by bishops.
Historians link the devotional revolution to the Famine and to emigration, arguing that the Famine strengthened clerical influence over the people who remained.

notes.h: Protestant identity: evangelicalism and the Orange Order
notes.b: Protestant identity in Ireland was shaped by evangelical revival and by the Orange Order, which defined loyalty to the Union and to Protestant supremacy.
points: Evangelicalism was a movement of Protestant revival that stressed personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary activity, and it spread among Protestants in the 1820s and 1830s.
The Second Reformation was the name given to the evangelical campaign to convert Catholics to Protestantism, carried out through missions, schools and Bible societies.
The Orange Order, founded in 1795, linked Protestant identity to loyalty to the Crown and to the Union, and it held public processions to show its strength.
The Church of Ireland was the established church until 1871, and its clergy and members saw evangelicalism as a means of defending their position against Catholic growth.
Protestant identity was strongest in Ulster, and it was reinforced by the growth of Belfast and by the sectarian divisions in its streets.

notes.h: The nation and the decline of the Irish language
notes.b: Nationalist writers, especially in Young Ireland, defined the nation through culture and history, while the Irish language declined in the same years.
points: Young Ireland's concept of the nation drew on Irish history and culture, and it was presented as a community that could include Protestants as well as Catholics.
Thomas Davis, whose life and work are covered in the notes on O'Connell and Young Ireland, argued that the nation should be united by culture rather than religion.
The Irish language was spoken mainly in the west, south-west and parts of the north-west, and it was weakened by the Famine, which killed and dispersed many of its speakers.
The national school system taught in English, and the spread of English-language education was a major factor in the decline of Irish.
Cultural nationalism in the 1840s and 1850s encouraged the study of Irish history and antiquities, but it did not reverse the decline of the language.

notes.b: Cullen was the leading figure in the Romanisation of Irish Catholicism, and his influence on politics and religion lasted for decades.
points: Paul Cullen was born in County Kildare in 1803 and was educated for the priesthood in Rome, where he worked in the Irish College and in Roman church administration.
He served as rector of the Irish College in Rome before his appointment as Archbishop of Armagh in 1849, when he returned to Ireland.
He was made a cardinal in 1866, and in the same year he was appointed Apostolic Delegate, the papal representative in Ireland.
He moved to the see of Dublin in 1852 and became the leading Catholic prelate in Ireland, a position he held until his death.
He presided over the Synod of Thurles in 1850, which set out a national programme for Catholic church discipline, and he worked to reform the education and practice of the clergy.
He opposed the Queen's Colleges and supported the Catholic University, and he was a strong opponent of the Fenian movement, which he condemned publicly.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters praised his organisation and his loyalty to Rome, and critics saw him as an autocrat who used his power to influence politics.
Later historians have judged his influence as central to the Romanisation of Irish Catholicism, and they have debated how far his policies shaped the political attitudes of the Catholic majority.

notes.h: Case study: the Synod of Thurles, 1850
notes.b: The Synod of Thurles was the first national synod of the Irish Catholic Church in about two centuries, and it set out a programme that aligned Irish practice with Rome.
points: Background: the Catholic Church in Ireland had no national synod for about two centuries, and it was run by bishops working in their own dioceses, with uneven discipline.
The Synod was called by Cardinal Cullen, then Archbishop of Armagh, and it met at Thurles in County Tipperary in August 1850.
The Synod issued decrees on the sacraments, on clerical discipline, on the education of priests and on the regulation of church property and marriage.
It condemned the Queen's Colleges, which were non-denominational, and it insisted that Catholics should attend Catholic institutions where possible.
The Synod's decrees were opposed by some bishops and by many lay Catholics who had supported the Queen's Colleges, and the debate over them continued for years.
The Synod's programme was carried forward by Cullen in Dublin from 1852, and it shaped the regular organisation of the Irish Church for the rest of the century.
Outcomes: the Catholic Church became more uniform in practice and in organisation, and its links with Rome became closer, a process known as Romanisation.
Significance: historians see the Synod as the first step in the reform and centralisation of the Irish Church, and they debate its impact on Catholic politics and on the Catholic University.

notes.h: Ultramontanism and the Romanisation of Irish Catholicism
notes.b: Ultramontanism, the movement that stressed papal authority, guided the reforms of the 1850s and 1860s.
points: Ultramontanism stressed the authority of the pope over national churches and local bishops, and it was strong in Rome and in many European countries after 1830.
In Ireland it meant closer control of parish life, uniform devotional practice and the discipline of clergy and laity through the bishops.
The Catholic University of Ireland, founded in 1854 with John Henry Newman as its first rector, was intended to provide a Catholic higher education under the Church's direction.
Ultramontanism also shaped Catholic attitudes to politics, encouraging support for the Church's interests over nationalist movements such as Fenianism.

notes.b: Aikenhead founded the Religious Sisters of Charity and St Vincent's Hospital, and her work shaped Catholic philanthropy in Dublin.
points: Mary Aikenhead was born in Cork in 1787, and she was a Catholic religious woman who devoted her life to nursing and education.
She founded the Religious Sisters of Charity in 1815 in Dublin, and the order ran schools, hospitals and visiting services for the poor.
The order opened St Vincent's Hospital in Dublin in 1834, which became one of the city's major hospitals, and it cared for patients regardless of their means.
She was a participant in Catholic charitable work, and her congregation expanded through the 1840s and 1850s, including during the Famine.
Contemporaries admired her charitable work, though the order's independence from the bishops sometimes caused tension in the Church.
Later historians have judged her as a pioneer of Catholic nursing and women's religious life, and as a figure who shaped the social role of religious women in Ireland.

notes.b: Carleton wrote fiction about the rural Irish, and his novels and stories shaped the image of the peasantry in the nineteenth century.
points: William Carleton was born in County Tyrone in 1794 to a Catholic family, and he moved to Dublin in the 1820s to pursue a literary career.
His Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry, published in two series in 1830 and 1833, described the life of rural Ireland, including its religion and its disputes.
His later novels, including Fardorougha the Miser (1839), explored rural poverty, tenant life and family conflict.
Carleton was a writer rather than a political figure, and his work reflected the mixed attitudes of his time towards the peasantry.
Contemporaries praised his realism and his knowledge of rural life, and some Catholic critics criticised his portrayal of Catholic peasant life as hostile.
Later critics have judged him as an important realist writer, and they have debated whether his work exaggerated the failings of the peasantry.

notes.h: Thomas Davis and the cultural life of the nation
notes.b: Davis contributed to the creative arts through The Nation's poems and ballads, linking literature to a national identity; his political career is in the notes on O'Connell and Young Ireland.
points: Davis's ballads and poems were published in The Nation and were collected in volumes after his death, and many became part of the repertoire of Irish song.
His work on Irish history and culture encouraged the study of the past as a means of building national identity.
Contemporaries saw his cultural nationalism as a unifying force, while critics argued that it was too idealistic and too close to radical politics.
Later historians have judged his cultural contribution as one of the foundations of modern Irish nationalism, though his influence on the language movement was limited.

notes.h: The creative arts: literature, painting and antiquarian scholarship
notes.b: Irish writers, painters and antiquarians produced work that drew on history, folklore and the countryside.
points: Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies, published in parts from 1808 onwards, set Irish songs to music and were popular across Britain and the United States.
James Clarence Mangan wrote poetry drawing on Irish history and translations from Irish and other languages, and he was a contributor to nationalist journals.
George Petrie, the painter and antiquarian, collected Irish music and recorded antiquities, and he published his collection of Irish airs in the 1850s.
John O'Donovan and Eugene O'Curry worked for the Ordnance Survey in the 1830s and 1840s, recording Irish place names and manuscripts, and they helped to establish the study of Irish history.
The creative arts were shaped by the Famine, which led many writers to address emigration, poverty and the collapse of rural life.

notes.b: Irish scientists and engineers made advances in mathematics, astronomy and physics, and Ireland's universities and observatories supported their work.
points: William Rowan Hamilton, a mathematician at Trinity College Dublin, discovered quaternions in 1843 and worked on algebra and optics.
William Parsons, the 3rd Earl of Rosse, built the Leviathan of Parsonstown, a large reflecting telescope at Birr Castle, County Offaly, which was completed in 1845.
Nicholas Callan, a priest at Maynooth, invented the induction coil in 1836, and his work contributed to the development of electrical technology.
George Boole, a mathematician, became professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork in 1849, and his work on logic laid the foundations of Boolean algebra.
Robert Kane, a chemist, wrote The Industrial Resources of Ireland in 1844, which argued for the development of Irish industry through science and technology.
Science in Ireland was supported by the Royal Dublin Society and by the new Queen's Colleges, which offered laboratories and teaching in science.

notes.b: Judgements of Catholic and cultural change depend on whether the test is organisation and uniformity, or the diversity and reach of cultural life.
points: Achievement of Cullen's reforms: the Church became more uniform in practice, with a stronger clergy, more schools and closer links to Rome.
Limit of Cullen's reforms: the Synod and the Church's control of education caused conflict with some bishops, with the Queen's Colleges, and with lay Catholics.
Contemporary view: Protestant critics saw the devotional revolution as a form of papal domination, while Catholic supporters saw it as renewal.
Later view: historians have argued that the Church's reforms helped to shape a distinctive Catholic identity that became central to Irish nationalism.
Achievement of the creative arts: Carleton, Moore and the antiquarians recorded and shaped the image of Irish life, and the study of Irish history grew.
Limit of the creative arts: the Famine and emigration weakened the rural culture on which much of this work depended, and the Irish language continued to decline.

keyTerms.definition: The movement that stressed the authority of the pope over national churches and bishops, which guided the Romanisation of Irish Catholicism after 1850.
A Protestant revival movement that stressed personal conversion, Bible reading and missionary work, and that spread among Irish Protestants in the 1820s and 1830s.
A community bound by shared history, culture and language, which Young Ireland used to define Irish nationality through literature and song.
Hostility and rivalry between religious communities, which shaped religious identities, public processions and urban life, especially in Belfast.
The national synod of the Irish Catholic Church held at Thurles in 1850 under Cullen, which set out a programme of discipline and reform.
The reform of Irish Catholic practice after the 1830s, marked by church building, regular Mass attendance, and closer control by bishops and clergy.
The process by which the Irish Catholic Church adopted more uniform practice and closer links with Rome, especially after the Synod of Thurles.
